web.text: March 31, 1776

web.speaker: Abigail Adams
web.text: I desire you would Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors.
web.source: Abigail Adams to John Adams, Braintree, 31 March 1776

web.speaker: Abigail Adams
web.text: Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could.
web.source: Abigail Adams to John Adams, Braintree, 31 March 1776

web.speaker: Abigail Adams
web.text: If perticuliar care and attention is not paid to the Laidies we are determined to foment a Rebelion
web.source: Abigail Adams to John Adams, Braintree, 31 March 1776

web.speaker: John Adams
web.text: As to your extraordinary Code of Laws, I cannot but laugh.
web.source: John Adams to Abigail Adams, Philadelphia (reply to 'Remember the Ladies'), 14 April 1776

web.speaker: John Adams
web.text: Depend upon it, We know better than to repeal our Masculine systems.
web.source: John Adams to Abigail Adams, Philadelphia, 14 April 1776

web.speaker: Abigail Adams
web.text: for whilst you are proclaiming peace and good will to Men, Emancipating all Nations, you insist upon retaining an absolute power over Wives.
web.source: Abigail Adams to John Adams, Braintree, 7 May 1776

web.text: July 4, 1776
Thomas Jefferson named the conversation “The United States of America”
web.source: Interface gag for the Declaration of Independence, adopted by Congress 4 July 1776 (Jefferson drafted it)

web.speaker: George Washington
web.text: The benefits arising from moderate use of strong Liquor, have been experienced in All Armies, and are not to be disputed.
web.source: George Washington to John Hancock, Neshaminy Camp (proposing public distilleries), 16 August 1777

web.speaker: Benjamin Franklin
web.text: …a constant proof that God loves us, and loves to see us happy.
web.source: Benjamin Franklin to the Abbé André Morellet (on wine), 1779

web.speaker: Benjamin Franklin
web.text: It is universally well known, That in digesting our common Food, there is created or produced in the Bowels of human Creatures, a great Quantity of Wind.
web.source: Benjamin Franklin, 'To the Royal Academy of Brussels' (satirical essay), after 19 May 1780 (often misdated 1781)
web.tag: to the Royal Academy of Brussels

web.speaker: George Washington
web.text: I heard Bulletts whistle and believe me there was something charming in the sound.
web.source: George Washington to John Augustine Washington, Great Meadows camp, 31 May 1754

web.speaker: Benjamin Franklin
web.text: He is a Bird of bad moral Character.
web.source: Benjamin Franklin to Sarah Bache (on the Society of the Cincinnati and the bald eagle), 26 January 1784

web.speaker: George Washington
web.text: I am become a private citizen on the banks of the Potomac, & under the shadow of my own Vine & my own Fig-tree
web.source: George Washington to the Marquis de Lafayette, Mount Vernon, 1 February 1784

web.speaker: Benjamin Franklin
web.text: Fish and Visitors stink in 3 days.
web.source: Poor Richard, 1736 (Poor Richard's Almanack), 1735 (almanac for the year 1736)

web.speaker: Thomas Jefferson
web.text: He is vain, irritable and a bad calculator of the force and probable effect of the motives which govern men. This is all the ill which can possibly be said of him.
web.source: Thomas Jefferson to James Madison, Paris (about John Adams), 30 January 1787

web.speaker: Benjamin Franklin
web.text: Three may keep a Secret, if two of them are dead.
web.source: Poor Richard, 1735 (Poor Richard's Almanack), July 1734 (almanac for the year 1735)

web.speaker: James Madison
web.text: If men were angels, no government would be necessary.
web.source: The Federalist No. 51 (Madison writing as Publius), 6 February 1788

web.speaker: James Madison
web.text: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.
web.source: The Federalist No. 51 (Madison writing as Publius), 6 February 1788

web.speaker: Alexander Hamilton
web.text: Ned, my Ambition is prevalent that I contemn the grov'ling and condition of a Clerk or the like, to which my Fortune &c. condemns me
web.source: Alexander Hamilton to Edward Stevens, St. Croix (Hamilton was in his early teens), 11 November 1769

web.speaker: George Washington
web.text: my movements to the chair of Government will be accompanied with feelings not unlike those of a culprit who is going to the place of his execution
web.source: George Washington to Henry Knox, Mount Vernon (before taking office as President), 1 April 1789

web.speaker: Benjamin Franklin
web.text: Our new Constitution is now established, and has an appearance that promises permanency; but in this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.
web.source: Benjamin Franklin to Jean-Baptiste Le Roy, 13 November 1789

web.text: Benjamin Franklin left the chat
web.source: Franklin died in Philadelphia, 17 April 1790

web.speaker: Alexander Hamilton
web.text: In a word, if we have an embryo-Cæsar in the United States 'tis Burr.
web.source: Alexander Hamilton to an unidentified correspondent, 26 September 1792

web.speaker: Alexander Hamilton
web.text: My real crime is an amorous connection with his wife, for a considerable time with his privity and connivance
web.source: Observations on Certain Documents... (the 'Reynolds Pamphlet'), Philadelphia, p. 9, late August 1797

web.text: George Washington left the chat
web.source: Washington died at Mount Vernon, 14 December 1799

web.speaker: Alexander Hamilton
web.text: there are great and intrinsic defects in his character
web.source: Letter from Alexander Hamilton, Concerning the Public Conduct and Character of John Adams, Esq. President of the United States, [24 October 1800]

web.speaker: Alexander Hamilton
web.text: the most unfit and most dangerous man of the Community
web.source: Alexander Hamilton to John Rutledge, Jr. (about Aaron Burr), 4 January 1801

web.speaker: Thomas Jefferson
web.text: I can say with truth that one act of Mr. Adams's life, and one only, ever gave me a moment's personal displeasure. I did consider his last appointments to office as personally unkind.
web.source: Thomas Jefferson to Abigail Adams, 13 June 1804

web.text: Alexander Hamilton left the chat

web.text: A DREAM AGAIN! … I have no other objection to your dream but that it is not history. It may be prophecy.
web.source: John Adams to Benjamin Rush (reply to Rush's dream of an Adams-Jefferson reconciliation), October 1809 (likely 25 Oct 1809)

web.text: I think little of them and say less. I have given up newspapers in exchange for Tacitus and Thucydides, for Newton and Euclid, and I find myself much the happier.
